argument: Descartes's proof of God's existence was never aimed at converting anyone to Christianity specifically; he needed only an infinite, perfect being as a metaphysical bookend for his rationalist system, since an unending chain of causal and logical connections would otherwise have no valid endpoint. That God also solves the Cartesian circle by guaranteeing that clear and distinct perceptions we're no longer directly attending to remain trustworthy, though critics point out that his formal/objective reality argument is itself circular and that his claim of an innate idea of an infinite God is undermined by cultures that believed in finite creators.
keyIdeas: Descartes was not trying to prove that the Christian or any specific God exists, only that some infinite first cause exists, as a metaphysical bookend for his rationalist system.

God's guarantee in Descartes's system is only needed to preserve truths we're no longer directly attending to (illustrated by the UPS delivery guy assuming the porch stairs haven't changed), not truths we clearly and distinctly perceive in the moment.
Because an infinite, perfect being would never deceive us, God's existence guarantees that our perceptions match reality, which is how Descartes escapes the problem posed by the evil demon.

Descartes needs God as a bookend because his rationalist project connects everything through causal and logical relationships, and an unending chain with no endpoint would make the whole system of connections invalid.

The 'Cartesian circle' objection: Descartes uses God to guarantee non-deceptive thoughts, but relies on non-deceptive thoughts to conclude that God exists in the first place; critics also object that his formal/objective reality distinction inconsistently treats ideas as both lesser and greater than finite things, and that many cultures believed in finite creators, suggesting the idea of an infinite God is taught rather than innate.
